rendered:
No, the collection does not show this. None of the documents describes using an ethylene glycol and polyethylene glycol mixture to extract critical materials from magnets. The word "magnet" appears only in unrelated contexts. The closest material is the following.

1. Ethylene glycol alone is used in the battery-recycling paper to delaminate electrode coatings from aluminum foil, not to extract metals from magnets.[1] 
2. A review notes that a choline chloride and ethylene glycol green solvent was used to recover, as the document puts it, "ethylene glycol was used to recover more than 90% of cobalt[2]" from LCO cathodes. This concerns battery cathodes, not magnets.

3. Polyethylene glycol appears only as a component of a PANI-PEG coating on cathode particles, not as a solvent for extraction. glycol (PEG) and the excellent electronic conductivity of polyaniline[3]

4. Magnetic separation appears only as a step to remove steel casings and other parts from spent batteries. including sieving, magnetic separation, and density separation[4]

So the documents do not establish whether an ethylene glycol and polyethylene glycol mixture could extract critical materials from magnets. Answering that would need a source outside this collection.
